source.title: Bagging in overparameterized learning: Risk characterization and risk monotonization
source.authors: Pratik V. Patil; Jin-Hong Du; A. Kuchibhotla

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplement are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives risk behavior for ridge and ridgeless linear predictors and shows that cross-validated bagging can monotonize risk as the data aspect ratio changes. This refines the scope of sample-wise double descent rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's own asymptotic analyses and illustrations of M=1 risks bear on V3; its cross-validated bagging results also report when the risk profile is monotonized. Background descriptions of double descent and findings attributed to other papers are not recorded as rows. Figure-only risk curves are recorded as such; no numerical values are inferred from them.
record.test_reason: Under proportional asymptotics, the paper derives and simulates the risk of ridge and ridgeless predictors as subsample size k varies at fixed p (M=1 curves). These show the sample-wise peak, so more data hurts near the interpolation threshold. The paper then proves that cross-validated subsample-size tuning (with bagging) makes risk monotone in the aspect ratio. The authors argue the hurt comes from using a procedure as-is, not from more data itself. That is a specific restatement of V3's scope and bears on V6's 'disappears under optimal tuning' clause. The setting is linear models, not deep networks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that properly tuned subagging always beats splagging. They find the optimal subsample size is below p, so bagged interpolators beat the full-data ridgeless predictor even when n>p. They show optimal subagged ridgeless matches optimal ridge under isotropy. The cross-validated bagged risk is provably monotone in ϕ, so more data cannot hurt the tuned procedure. All of this holds under a well-specified linear model.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes asymptotic squared prediction risk for bagged ridge and ridgeless linear predictors and cross-validated subsample selection; it does not reproduce the original deep-network experiments or their model-size and epoch sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported risk profiles vary with predictor type (ridge versus ridgeless), regularization, subsample aspect ratio, number of bags, and data aspect ratio. Cross-validated subagging and splagging have distinct risk profiles.

fits_no_version.finding: Under optimal subagging, the best subsample aspect ratio is always above 1, so bagged interpolators beat least squares even when n>p.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ensembles of interpolating subsample fits outperform full-data least squares in the underparameterised regime.

record.problems: The risk-curve illustrations use linear models, not deep networks. The M=1 curves relevant to the unbagged sample-size behavior are figure-only in the reported examples, with no curve values extracted. The theory relies on a well-specified linear model and Assumptions 1–5; the paper notes a nonlinear simulation but does not use it to establish the general claim.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-bearing reported results were omitted. Numerical risk curves for bagged predictors with M>1 and other subsample conditions are not separate rows here because they do not directly measure the unbagged sample-size behavior in V3.

untested.parts: No deep networks and no model-size sweep of networks.
Only well-specified linear ridge and ridgeless models, with one nonlinear-response simulation. Deep networks are not tested.
No sweep across model classes. Only the linear p/n axis, which the paper reads as a sample axis.
Not tested: whether label noise drives the peak, whether peaks split into several, and whether optimally tuned ridge λ removes the peak under general covariance (Remark 5.4 leaves this open).

missing.what: Unbagged full-data ridgeless risk versus data aspect ratio ϕ (dashed curves). This is the classical sample-wise and p-wise double-descent curve that the paper itself plots.
missing.versions: V3; V4 if the p/n axis is read as capacity

missing.what: Finite-sample slight non-monotonicity of the cross-validated M=1 risk profile, which the authors attribute to small sample size.
Optimal subagged ridgeless risk equals optimal ridge risk for isotropic features; monotonicity of optimal ridge under general covariance is left open.
Nonlinear-response simulation: M=1 subagged ridgeless risk versus ϕs shows the same non-monotone pattern.

record.verdict_notes: The M=1 sample-wise risk curves are re-derivations of known results (Hastie et al.; Patil et al. 2022b). The paper's novelty is the bagged risk and the monotonisation. Rows r5–r8 carry two versions with one state: 'absent' refers to the peak. That restricts V3's scope and matches V6's disappearance clause. It is not a challenge to either. Neither original source is this paper.

versions.untested_parts: Model-wise double descent in deep networks; no sweep over deep-network size.
Epoch-wise double descent; no sweep over training epochs.
The paper studies linear ridge and ridgeless predictors, including subsample-size and data-aspect-ratio risk profiles; it does not test arbitrary models or settings.
No capacity sweep across model classes testing second descent past interpolation.
No single effective-complexity measure is proposed and tested as predicting peak locations across axes.
The paper does not test whether label noise drives the peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimal regularization makes such peaks disappear.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameter number or test of the resulting curve shape.

rows.subject: ridgeless predictor (λ = 0)
rows.operation_detail: Risk curve over subsample aspect ratio ϕs, corresponding to varying subsample size k, at fixed full-data aspect ratio.
rows.measure: Prediction risk as subsample aspect ratio varies; the text identifies non-monotonic risk behavior for the underlying ridgeless predictor.
rows.note: The figure plots limiting risk against ϕs. The text describes non-monotonic risk for the underlying predictor but does not give curve values.
rows.check: Figure-only. The text (Remark 3.4) states that ridgeless variance diverges as ϕs→1 for finite M, so the M=1 risk peaks at k=p. Increasing k toward p raises risk. The M=1 risk characterisation is credited to Patil et al. (2022b); here it is re-derived and simulated (p=500, 100 repetitions).

rows.subject: ridgeless predictor (λ = 0)
rows.size_stated: p and n grow proportionally; p/n → ϕ
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical risk profile of the cross-validated subagged predictor, optimized over subsample aspect ratio as data aspect ratio varies.
rows.measure: Limiting prediction risk versus data aspect ratio; the optimized risk is monotonically increasing in ϕ, so it decreases as sample size increases at fixed p.
rows.note: This is a result for the modified, cross-validated bagged procedure, not the unbagged predictor.
rows.check: The sample-wise peak is absent for the cross-validated subagged ridgeless predictor (Theorem 4.5). This is a modified, tuned procedure. For V3 the result restricts scope rather than challenging it. For V6 the absence is the 'disappears under tuning' clause holding, with subsample size as the tuned quantity rather than λ. Theorem 4.1 gives the general version.

source_check.correct: For subagged ridgeless predictors, the oracle envelope F(ϕ)=min_{ϕs≥ϕ} R_sub(ϕ,ϕs) is nondecreasing in ϕ. Theorem 4.5 establishes (R_CV−F(ϕ))_+→0 in probability, rather than exact convergence to F. Under Assumptions 1–5 the stated guarantee uses Algorithm 1 with CEN=MOM. Exact convergence requires the stronger uniform-in-subsample-size assumptions in Remark 4.3. State absent applies to the oracle envelope; state cannot_determine applies to monotonicity of the actual CV risk from this theorem alone.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1, Remarks 4.3–4.4; Section 4.2, Theorem 4.5, equation (35), and footnote 6.
source_check.problem: The row assigns oracle-envelope monotonicity to actual cross-validated risk and omits the MOM condition.

relation.reason: Its own risk characterizations, optimization results, and simulations directly address sample-wise double descent and its dependence on tuning.

tranche.reason: The study characterizes sample-wise nonmonotonicity and shows how subsample optimization removes it from the oracle risk profile, qualifying V3 and supporting V6's disappearance clause.

source_check.notes: The supplied source is arXiv v3 from October 2023. The authors-conclusion paraphrase also needs qualification: Proposition 4.6 proves non-strict dominance over optimal splagging, and Proposition 4.7 includes zero-signal and noiseless exceptions to universal strict improvement and k<p.

statements.correction: Theorem 4.5: optimized limiting risk nondecreasing in ϕ for each M; positive excess of CV risk over that envelope converges to zero in probability; CEN=MOM under Assumptions 1–5. Remark 4.3: stronger uniform assumptions needed for exact convergence.
statements.problem: Subsample optimization gives a monotonic oracle risk envelope, but cross-validation is only proved asymptotically no worse than that envelope under the stated assumptions. This does not itself establish monotonicity of actual CV risk.

statements.correction: Oracle subsample-optimized limiting risk is nondecreasing in ϕ. Cross-validated risk has a one-sided asymptotic bound relative to this envelope; exact convergence requires stronger uniform assumptions.
statements.problem: The statement conflates oracle subsample optimization with the weaker guarantee proved for cross-validated selection.
